EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Project Abstract & Table of Contents

Seasonal flash flooding across the low-lying catchment basins of Sri Lanka's North Western Province—notably along the Deduru Oya and Tabbowa reservoir cascades in the Puttalam District—frequently causes acute humanitarian, agricultural, and socio-economic devastation. Post-disaster assessments conducted by the Disaster Management Centre (DMC) reveal that while dam masonry remains structurally sound, emergency spillway operations suffer from critical human and procedural latencies. During intense monsoonal depressions, manual telephone verification chains and mechanical gate winches can take 30 to 45 minutes from threshold breach to physical water release, compressing downstream evacuation windows.

The Smart Dam Alert System with Automated Gate Control (SDAS) overcomes these vulnerabilities through a resilient, four-tier engineering infrastructure:

  • Local Autonomous Safety Loop (Tier 1): Deterministic embedded execution on an ESP32 dual-core SoC running FreeRTOS, performing dual ultrasonic sensing, dynamic acoustic velocity temperature compensation, plausibility voting, and closed-loop gate positioning completely offline without cloud dependencies.
  • Cellular Emergency Dispatch (Tier 2): Hardware-driven, staged SMS broadcasting via an isolated SIM800L GSM quad-band module, alerting emergency authorities (DMC, Police, Community Leaders) within 30 seconds of risk escalation.
  • Cloud Telemetry & Authenticated Remote Command (Tier 3): Real-time bi-directional telemetry synchronisation via Supabase PostgreSQL and sub-2-second remote manual operator overrides over an authenticated MQTT broker.
  • Predictive Machine Learning Microservice (Tier 4): An external Python FastAPI server utilizing LSTM recurrent networks for 1-hour ahead water-level forecasting and Autoencoders for transducer drift anomaly detection.
Core Academic Innovation: True Local Autonomy with Zero Single-Point-of-Failure
Even in the event of catastrophic Wi-Fi loss, cellular data drop, or cloud backend outage, the dam continues to sample water levels, execute acoustic compensation, actuate the sluice gate, and sound emergency sirens locally and autonomously.

1.2 Cloud Database & Machine Learning Architecture

The system employs a high-reliability dual-cloud integration stack:

  • Supabase PostgreSQL Cloud: Provides structured storage for telemetry_logs (sampling water distance, temperature, humidity, computed water level, gate angle), alert_events (audit trail of state transitions), and operator_commands. Secured by strict Row Level Security (RLS): the public role possesses read-only access, while authenticated station operators can insert control override records.
  • Low-Latency MQTT Broker: A dedicated broker handles sub-2-second command latency for physical manual overrides (OPEN_10, CLOSE_10, ESTOP) and publishes telemetry summaries every 2 seconds.
  • Predictive ML Microservice (FastAPI): An asynchronous Python service that queries telemetry every 60 seconds. An LSTM network trained on monsoonal catchment inflow profiles predicts water levels 1 hour in advance. An Autoencoder reconstructs dual ultrasonic readings to detect transducer bio-fouling or structural drift (z-score > 3.0).

1.3 Mobile Application Ecosystem (React Native / Expo)

To ensure absolute cyber security and prevent unauthorized gate manipulation, SDAS implements strict role segregation into two separate applications:

  1. Public Disaster Portal (Login-Free): Designed for downstream villagers, farmers, and motorists. Displays real-time dam water levels (circular gauge), alert state banners, emergency hotline numbers, and safety tips in English, Sinhala, and Tamil. No actuation code exists in this app.
  2. Operator Command Interface (Authenticated): Restricted to authorized irrigation engineers and DMC staff. Features biometric login, two-factor authentication (2FA), manual gate incremental controls (+10% / -10%), instant E-STOP trigger, and an immutable cryptographic audit log recording every operator keystroke.
SECTION 2: AUDITING, PROBLEM SOLVING & FIXES

2. What We Did — Engineering Journey & Bug Fixes

During the comprehensive system audit of the prototype firmware and hardware schematics, our team identified 6 critical firmware bugs, 10 secondary software defects, and several hardware schematic contradictions that would have prevented the system from operating reliably during a flash flood. Below is the complete record of what was identified and how we engineered the solutions.

2.1 Critical Defects Identified & Rectified

1. SMS Alerts Failed to Dispatch (Fixed in gsm_modem.cpp)

Root Cause: The original GSMManager::update() function began every execution cycle by executing a tight while (serial.available()) serial.read(); loop, discarding all incoming bytes on UART2. Consequently, when an SMS send command (AT+CMGS) was issued, the modem's > input prompt and subsequent OK confirmation were discarded before the state machine could parse them. Every SMS timed out, was dropped from the queue, and never retried.

Engineering Fix: We eliminated the blind buffer drain and restricted UART buffer flushing strictly to the TX_IDLE state. Added explicit state handling for the > character and acknowledgment timeouts.

2. SMS Queue Dropped Danger Alerts (Fixed in gsm_modem.h)

Root Cause: The outbound SMS queue was statically sized to hold only 6 messages. However, broadcasting a single flood alert dispatches 4 messages (Station Engineer, Police, DMC, Community Leader). If a CLEAR_AREA alert fired and water quickly surged into DANGER, the queue overflowed and silently dropped the critical DANGER messages.

Engineering Fix: Expanded queue capacity to 16 slots, implemented circular ring-buffer semantics, and instituted a priority-insertion algorithm where DANGER and ESTOP messages pre-empt low-priority routine telemetry messages.

3. E-STOP Failed to Stop Sluice Gate Instantly (Fixed in actuators.cpp)

Root Cause: Pressing the physical E-STOP button or sending the MQTT ESTOP command merely toggled an internal software boolean. The servo was only halted inside evaluate(), which executed every 2.0 seconds. Because the servo steps 1.0° every 15 ms, the gate could travel the entire 0° → 90° sweep before halting.

Engineering Fix: Refactored triggerEmergencyStop() to instantly freeze targetAngle = currentAngle, detach the PWM timer if necessary, assert the active alarm buzzer, and attach a hardware interrupt (ISR) directly to GPIO22 for sub-millisecond physical response.

4. Main Control Loop Blocked by Cloud Outages (Fixed in network_telemetry.cpp)

Root Cause: Supabase HTTPS POST and MQTT connect() were blocking network calls executed in the single Arduino loop(). When Wi-Fi disconnected or HiveMQ lagged, the CPU stalled for 5 to 10 seconds. During this freeze, the servo motor, ultrasonic sensors, emergency buzzer, and buttons were completely non-functional.

Engineering Fix: Migrated to a dual-core FreeRTOS architecture. Core 0 is dedicated exclusively to Wi-Fi, Supabase HTTPS, and MQTT networking. Core 1 deterministically executes the 100 ms sensor acquisition, acoustic compensation, and servo control loop with zero network interruption.

5. Rising Flood Reported as Sensor Fault (Fixed in sensors.cpp & Mounting)

Root Cause: The previous design utilized JSN-SR04T sensors with a large 20–25 cm blind zone mounted only 65 cm high. When water rose above 45 cm (distance < 20 cm), both sensors returned invalid echo timeouts. The firmware flagged a critical_sensor_fault and locked the sluice gate closed instead of opening it!

Engineering Fix: Replaced sensors with standard HC-SR04 ultrasonic modules (blind zone ≤ 2.0 cm). Mounted sensors at 50.0 cm above the channel floor (giving 10 cm safety headroom at 100% capacity). Programmed the firmware to treat any distance reading < 2.0 cm as 100% Full / CRITICAL DANGER, never as a sensor fault.

6. Gate Over-Discharge & Unsecured Commands (Fixed in state_machine.cpp & config.h)

Root Cause: The system defined GATE_PCT_MAX_LIMIT as 50% but never enforced it in code, allowing an MQTT OPEN_100 command to open the sluice gate to 100% (180°). In a reservoir cascade, a 100% gate opening produces destructive downstream flooding and risks mechanical gate jam.

Engineering Fix: Hard-coded an inviolable clamp in setTargetGatePercent(): targetPercent = constrain(targetPercent, 0, 50). Disallowed 100% gate opening under all operational modes.

SECTION 3.3: POWER SUPPLY ARCHITECTURE

3.3 XL4015 Dual-Rail Power Routing & Isolation

One of the most frequent points of failure in amateur IoT projects is powering high-power inductive actuators (servo motors) and pulsed RF transmitters (GSM modems) from the microcontroller's 3.3V or 5V development board pins. Under load, this causes immediate brownout resets. SDAS implements a strictly isolated dual-rail architecture using two parallel XL4015 5A buck converters.

Acoustic Velocity Temperature Compensation Mathematics

The speed of sound in dry air varies non-linearly with atmospheric temperature. A temperature change of 10°C shifts acoustic velocity by nearly 6 m/s, introducing up to ±8 cm of error in uncompensated ultrasonic distance measurements. SDAS acquires ambient temperature T_DHT from the DHT22 sensor and recalculates the true acoustic velocity in real time:

v(T) = 331.4 + (0.606 * T_DHT) [meters per second]

Given the round-trip echo pulse duration t_echo (in microseconds) returned by the HC-SR04 timer, the true one-way physical distance D to the water surface is calculated as:

D = (v(T) * t_echo) / (2.0 * 10000.0) [centimeters]

With the sensors securely mounted at height H_mount = 50.0 cm above the channel bed and an ultrasonic physical blind zone H_blind = 2.0 cm, the effective water depth h_water and reservoir percentage are computed as:

h_water = H_mount - D = 50.0 - D [centimeters] Water_Percent = constrain( ( (H_mount - D) / (H_mount - H_blind) ) * 100.0, 0.0, 100.0 )

Dual-Sensor Plausibility Cross-Validation Voting

To prevent false gate actuations caused by acoustic surface ripples, floating debris, or component failure, SDAS cross-validates readings from HC-SR04 #1 (D1) and HC-SR04 #2 (D2):

  1. If |D1 - D2| ≤ 5.0 cm: Both sensors agree. The system computes the authoritative distance as the arithmetic mean D_avg = (D1 + D2) / 2. System state remains in NORMAL OPERATIONAL MODE.
  2. If |D1 - D2| > 5.0 cm: Plausibility violation detected. The system transitions immediately to DEGRADED MODE:
    • The sluice gate freezes its current physical position (no automated motion allowed).
    • The RGB LED switches to PULSING BLUE.
    • A degraded-mode diagnostic alert is uploaded to Supabase and dispatched via SMS to the Station Engineer.
    • The system selects the conservative (higher water level / smaller distance) reading for safety warnings.
  3. If both sensors timeout or report D < 2.0 cm: The water level has reached the upper rim (100% capacity). The system triggers STAGE 3 DANGER immediately.

4.2 Slew-Rate Clamped Gate Actuation

Sudden sluice gate displacement generates hydraulic water hammer pressure waves that erode riverbanks and risk physical gate jamming. The SDAS firmware implements a software-regulated slew-rate limiter:

  • The servo never steps directly from 0° → 90°.
  • Instead, the control loop advances the servo angle by 1.0° every 15 ms.
  • Transitioning from 0% (0°) to 20% (36°) requires exactly 540 ms of smooth, controlled travel.
  • Transitioning to 50% (90°) requires 1.35 seconds, ensuring gradual hydraulic discharge without surge shocks.

4.3 Multimeter Calibration & Bench Testing Checklist

Before connecting sensitive semiconductor modules to power rails, perform this mandatory 6-step bench trimming:

  1. Isolate downstream modules: Unplug the ESP32, SIM800L, MG90S servo, and sensors. (Factory XL4015 modules often output 12V–18V uncalibrated, which will immediately burn your components).
  2. Power up 12V supply: Connect the 12V 5A adapter to IN+ and IN- of both buck converters. Turn ON the SPST switch.
  3. Trim Buck #1 to +5.00V: Place DMM probes on Buck #1 OUT+ and OUT-. Turn the brass screw on the blue potentiometer counter-clockwise until the multimeter reads 5.00V ± 0.05V.
  4. Trim Buck #2 to +4.00V: Move DMM probes to Buck #2 OUT+ and OUT-. Turn the brass screw counter-clockwise until the multimeter reads 4.00V ± 0.05V.
  5. Verify capacitor orientation: Ensure the 1000 µF low-ESR capacitor is connected across SIM800L VCC and GND with correct polarity (negative stripe to GND).
  6. Connect and verify under load: Power OFF, wire all modules according to the color chart, power back ON, and verify that Buck #1 stays ≥ 4.90V during servo motion, and Buck #2 stays ≥ 3.60V during SMS bursts.
SECTION 4.4: ACADEMIC DEFENSE MANUAL

4.4 Viva Defense Q&A: Top 10 Technical Questions & Answers

During your final project defense, university examiners typically test hardware rationale, safety fail-safes, concurrency, and real-world failure modes. Below are the 10 most critical viva questions with authoritative answers:

Q1: Why did you use two XL4015 buck converters instead of powering everything from a single 5V regulator or the ESP32's onboard LDO?

Answer: The SIM800L cellular module draws 2.0A peak current bursts during 2G TDMA radio transmission (lasting 577 µs), and operates optimally at 4.0V (maximum absolute rating 4.4V). Feeding it from 5V would permanently destroy the RF power amplifier, while feeding it from the ESP32's 3.3V LDO causes immediate under-voltage lockout (UVLO) resets. Furthermore, the MG90S servo motor generates severe inductive back-EMF spikes when starting or stalling. By dedicating Buck #2 exclusively to the SIM800L and Buck #1 to the servo, ESP32, and sensors, we achieve complete electrical isolation, preventing motor noise from dropping cellular calls.

Q2: What happens if both Wi-Fi and cellular connections fail simultaneously during a flash flood?

Answer: The dam continues to operate autonomously with 100% safety functionality. SDAS implements a Local Autonomous Safety Loop (Tier 1). The ESP32's Core 1 executes closed-loop sensing, acoustic velocity temperature compensation, sensor plausibility voting, servo gate positioning, and audible/visual alarms directly in hardware. Cloud and cellular connectivity are purely telemetry and notification layers—the physical safety of the dam has zero dependency on external networks.

Q3: Why did you mount the HC-SR04 sensors at 50 cm instead of lower down, and how do you handle the blind zone?

Answer: The HC-SR04 ultrasonic transducer has a physical acoustic blind zone of 2.0 cm. By mounting the sensors at 50.0 cm above the channel bed, at 100% reservoir capacity the water level reaches 40 cm, leaving 10 cm of safety headroom. This ensures the water surface never enters the acoustic transducer's blind zone during valid operations. Furthermore, our firmware includes a critical safeguard: if echo duration drops below 2.0 cm or timeouts occur, the system treats it as 100% capacity / DANGER rather than a sensor fault, ensuring the gate opens rather than remaining locked.

Q4: Why is temperature compensation essential for ultrasonic water level measurement?

Answer: The velocity of sound in air varies with temperature according to v(T) = 331.4 + (0.606 * T) m/s. In Sri Lanka's tropical climate, temperatures fluctuate between 22°C at night and 38°C at midday. Without dynamic compensation, an uncalibrated 343 m/s assumption causes measurement errors exceeding ±6 to 8 cm, which would trigger false gate openings or delayed emergency warnings. SDAS dynamically corrects sound velocity every 100 ms using live readings from the DHT22 climate sensor.

Q5: How does your FreeRTOS dual-core allocation prevent system lockups?

Answer: Traditional Arduino firmware runs in a single blocking thread. When HTTP POST requests to Supabase or MQTT reconnect calls experience network latency, the CPU blocks for up to 10 seconds, freezing servo motion and sensor sampling. By pinning network operations to Core 0 and real-time physical control (sensors, servo, buzzer, buttons) to Core 1, our control loop runs at a deterministic 100 ms cadence with zero jitter, completely immune to cloud or network lags.

Q6: Why is the sluice gate clamped to 50% maximum opening instead of 100%?

Answer: In hydrological dam cascade management, releasing 100% spillway volume suddenly causes catastrophic downstream bank overtopping and flash flooding, while simultaneously creating severe structural negative pressure (hydraulic suction) on the sluice gate rails. Our audited specification hard-clamps gate displacement to 50% (90° angle) under all conditions—both in autonomous automation and remote operator override—preventing hydraulic surges.

Q7: How do you prevent unauthorized users from opening the dam gate over the internet?

Answer: We engineered complete role segregation across the mobile application layer. The public disaster app contains no authentication tokens and zero actuator code—it interacts with Supabase exclusively through read-only Row Level Security (RLS) views. The operator app requires multi-factor authentication (MFA). Furthermore, manual operator overrides must pass through an encrypted MQTT topic with a strict 5-minute auto-revert watchdog timer. If an operator opens the gate manually and subsequently loses connection, the local controller automatically re-assumes autonomous control after 5 minutes.

Q8: What is the purpose of the 1N5819 Schottky diode between Buck #1 and ESP32 VIN?

Answer: When developers plug a MicroUSB cable into the ESP32 while the 12V bench power supply is active, 5V from Buck #1 and 5V from the computer's USB port are placed in parallel. If Buck #1 outputs 5.05V and the USB port is at 4.95V, current backfeeds into the PC's USB host controller, potentially frying the computer's motherboard. The 1N5819 Schottky diode has a low forward voltage drop (~0.3V) and strictly blocks reverse current into the PC.

Q9: Why are resistors of different values used for the RGB LED channels (220 Ω for Red, 100 Ω for Green/Blue)?

Answer: Red LED dies have a forward voltage drop (V_F) of approximately 1.9V to 2.0V, whereas Green and Blue dies have a higher V_F of 3.0V to 3.2V. Powered from 3.3V, a uniform resistor would cause Red to glow excessively bright and drown out Green/Blue. Using R_Red = 220 Ω yields I = (3.3 - 1.9)/220 ≈ 6.4 mA, while R_Grn/Blu = 100 Ω yields I = (3.3 - 3.0)/100 ≈ 3.0 mA. This produces balanced optical luminous intensity across all state colors.

Q10: What is the purpose of the 1kΩ / 2.2kΩ voltage divider on the SIM800L RXD pin?

Answer: The SIM800L serial interface operates at 2.8V CMOS logic levels, with internal ESD clamp diodes to its 2.8V rail. The ESP32 outputs 3.3V TTL on GPIO17 (TX2). Connecting them directly forces current through the modem's internal clamp diodes, degrading the silicon over time. The 1.0 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ voltage divider steps 3.3V down to 3.3 * (2.2 / (1.0 + 2.2)) ≈ 2.27 V, which safely meets the SIM800L high-level input threshold (V_IH ≥ 2.1 V) without overvoltage stress.
